title: Three times of prayer
hookLine: Shia usually combine the five prayers into three times of day, which Sunni schools allow in certain cases

lines: NOON, THEN AFTERNOON, BACK TO BACK.
A NEIGHBOR WAITS FOR THE SHADOWS.
cards: A family in Detroit finishes lunch, and someone lays out the prayer mats. They pray the noon prayer, then the afternoon prayer straight after it. That evening, the same: sunset, then night, back to back.
Their neighbor down the street, who also prays five times a day, waits for the afternoon prayer until the shadows grow long. Same Qur'an, same five prayers, same direction. Two different clocks.
Neither family is cutting corners. Each follows a school, and each school can show you its reasons.

teach.h: COMMON GROUND: PRAYER HAS FIXED HOURS.
teach.b: Start with the common ground. The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's words, "Lo! worship at fixed hours hath been enjoined on the believers." The prayers have times.
The question is how wide those times are.

teach.h: ONE VERSE, READ AS THREE MOMENTS.
teach.b: Next, a verse the schools read differently. In surah seventeen, the Qur'an tells the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ to establish prayer from the sun's decline until the dark of night, and the recitation at dawn.
Some readers hear three moments there: the decline of the sun, the dark of night, and dawn. Then a report.

teach.h: IBN ABBAS: JOINED, IN MEDINA, NO RAIN.
teach.b: In Sahih Muslim, Ibn Abbas says the Prophet prayed noon and afternoon together, and sunset and night together, in Medina, with no fear and no rain. Asked why, Ibn Abbas said he wanted no hardship for his community.
Ja'fari scholars, followed by Twelver Shia, read the verse and the report together: noon and afternoon share one stretch of time, and so do sunset and night.
Praying each at its own moment is good, they teach, and joining is permitted any day. So a Shia family can pray the five in three sittings: dawn, midday, evening.

teach.h: SUNNI SCHOOLS: JOIN FOR SET REASONS.
teach.b: The Sunni schools know the same report, and they also allow joining, called jam', but for set reasons. Shafi'i, Maliki and Hanbali scholars allow it on a journey, and some for heavy rain or illness.

Hanafi scholars allow it on pilgrimage, at Arafah and Muzdalifah. Otherwise, each prayer keeps its own time. Two readings of the same texts: one widens the time, the other keeps each prayer in its own.

how: Twelver Shia follow Ja'fari law, which lets noon and afternoon, and sunset and night, be prayed together, so the five prayers are often prayed in three sittings; Sunni schools join prayers for set reasons such as travel, rain, or the pilgrimage.

games.q: what does “three times of prayer” mean?
o: all five prayers, prayed in three sittings: dawn, midday, evening
only three daily prayers, said in place of the usual five
three set hours when the call to prayer is heard

games.q: three times of prayer — tap the pairs.
p: the common ground: prayer has times
joined prayers in Medina, no fear or rain

s: Shia Muslims pray only three prayers a day
they pray all five; Ja'fari law lets them be prayed in three sittings.
Sunni schools never allow joining two prayers
they allow it for set reasons: Shafi'i, Maliki and Hanbali scholars on a journey, Hanafi scholars at Arafah and Muzdalifah.
in a report in Sahih Muslim, the Prophet joined prayers in Medina with no fear and no rain
Ibn Abbas reports it and says the reason was to spare his community hardship.

games.q: you're with Ibn Abbas. someone asks why the Prophet joined noon and afternoon in Medina, with no journey, no fear, no rain. what does he answer?
o: he wanted no hardship for his community.
games.why: Ibn Abbas says the Prophet wanted no hardship for his community. the schools then read that report in different ways.

practice: Think back over yesterday and count, on your fingers, the moments your day paused: at dawn, at lunch, at a red light, or only at night.

If you pray, notice which prayers you pray in their own moment and which you gather together, and where your school draws that line; if you don't, notice where your day already stops, the places a prayer could sit.

wordCard.voice: Three times of prayer. In Ja'fari practice, the five prayers prayed in three sittings; in Sunni schools, joining allowed on a journey and for certain other needs. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: gathering, joining; in law, praying two prayers together in one time.

carryVoice: Your line: five in three. The clock can differ while the five stay the same. Same time tomorrow.
